transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-05-14
Time: 15:00 PDT
Duration: ~68 minutes
Attendees: Sofia (Redwood AE), Marcus (Redwood SE), Daniel (Redwood Infra), Priya (Aurelius Head of Platform), Tom (NetEng), Lina (ML infra), Alex (Security), Samir (SRE)

Summary: SE-led deep dive on private VPC networking and runtime implications. Discussed PrivateLink vs peering, NAT/egress, subnet sizing, internal DNS + Route53, and how network hops affect KV cache and batching latency.

Transcript:
[00:00] Sofia: Hey everyone thanks for joining, um this is the deep dive we've been planning, Marcus will lead on the runtime and I'll cover architecture and next steps. does that work?
[00:07] Priya: Yeah that works, thanks. Quick ask, we want to understand worst-case p99 latency when running in our private VPC, not just ave numbers.
[00:15] Marcus: yep, absolutely. We'll go over what adds to tail latency -- network hops, cold kv cache, batching delays, quantization overhead, and kernel selection.
[00:30] Tom: For networking, our biggest constraints are: no public IPs on model hosts, outbound egress is via a centralized NAT in a DMZ subnet, and we prefer PrivateLink for control plane connectivity.
[00:45] Marcus: ok that's good context. quick note, when using PrivateLink endpoints the control plane traffic goes over an ENI in your VPC, so that avoids NAT for control plane calls. Data plane with private deployment -- depends if you choose private control plane or fully air gapped.
[01:05] Daniel: to be clear, our private option runs the control plane components in Redwood-managed SaaS or in your VPC?
[01:12] Sofia: we have two patterns: 1) Private control plane, where control plane is in our infrastructure but communicates via PrivateLink endpoints in your VPC; 2) fully customer-hosted control plane (on-prem or VPC) — more effort, we ship the package. PrivateLink is common for enterprise customers.
[01:30] Tom: ok, so using PrivateLink avoids egress charging and NAT, yes?
[01:36] Marcus: It avoids the NAT hop for control plane; you still may have NAT for outbound to other third-party services. For model inference traffic, if the runtime lives in your VPC the traffic is local. if runtime in Redwood Dedicated, then there is network traversal and you'll see additional latency.
[01:58] Priya: we plan to host runtime in our VPC to meet data residency and compliance. main worry: will cross-az traffic for KV cache and batching blow up latency?
[02:10] Marcus: good question. KV cache in our runtime is local to process or node — it relies on shared memory + local disk for hot prefixes. when you have multi-node deployments across AZs, we recommend pinning inference pools to a single AZ for low-latency traffic; cross-AZ adds ~0.5-2ms on AWS depending on instance type and infra.
[02:33] Lina: are there configs to ensure requests hit warm caches? we see big p99 spikes when first keys miss.
[02:40] Marcus: yes, batching and intelligent prefix caching help. we do continuous batching with latency SLOs; the system will flush small batches if latency SLO is near. warmup passes or pre-warming KV cache with representative prompts helps. also consider model sharding and KV locality.
[03:02] Tom: on PrivateLink, do we need endpoint services and acceptance from your side? what's the setup flow?
[03:08] Sofia: yes you create an interface VPC endpoint and subscribe to our endpoint service. we accept the endpoint on our side. we'll provide a CloudFormation template to reduce manual steps. Marcus will attach a diagram.
[03:22] [Marcus - mumbles] i'll add the diagram showing ENIs, route tables, and security group flow.
[03:28] Alex: how does DNS resolution work for PrivateLink endpoints? route53 private hosted zones?
[03:33] Marcus: typically we provision a private hosted zone and put an alias for the endpoint DNS; you can override with your resolvers. note: some setups require split-horizon DNS if you have on-prem resolvers. we'll capture that in the network doc.
[03:50] Samir: what about egress to S3 for model artifacts and to KMS for key operations - that still goes through NAT right?
[03:57] Daniel: yes, unless you create VPC endpoints for S3 and KMS. strongly recommend gateway endpoint for S3 and interface endpoint for KMS to keep traffic in the AWS network.
[04:10] Priya: ok around runtime perf, how much does quantization help throughput and latency? we run 8-bit and some 4-bit stuff in research.
[04:18] Marcus: quantization reduces compute time and memory; for many transformer models, 8-bit gives modest latency improvements and big throughput gains; 4-bit is more model dependent and sometimes increases CPU/GPU kernel complexity. we provide quant profiles tuned per-model; I'll share quant benchmarks.
[04:38] Lina: any gotchas around quantized models and KV cache?
[04:42] Marcus: KV cache format is independent, but quantization changes token compute cost. larger batches amortize kernel overhead. important: make sure your batch size distribution in production matches the benchmark used for quant profiles.
[04:56] Tom: we do a lot of short requests with low token counts. batching helps but increases latency. what's your recommendation?
[05:02] Marcus: for short requests, use adaptive batching with tight latency SLOs. Redwood runtime can operate at target p95/p99 bounds and will avoid large batch waits if configured; batching gains are best with moderate request concurrency. also prefix caching reduces tokens generated per request which helps.
[05:20] Priya: curious about encryption and key management - is KMS used for model artifacts and ephemeral keys?
[05:27] Sofia: we support integrating your KMS for secrets and provide optional HSM support for enterprise customers. for private deployments you can point to your KMS endpoints via VPC interface endpoint.
[05:38] Alex: audit logs: do you store request traces in Redwood or can they remain in our S3?
[05:44] Sofia: for private runtime we can stream logs to your account (S3/CloudWatch) and provide audit metadata to your SIEM. by default, hosted logs live in Redwood but for Private we prefer customer-managed sinks.
[05:58] Marcus: back to network perf - routing tables matter. avoid SNAT where possible for high-throughput pods; ENIs with Security groups allow consistent ips. Also pick optimized instance types; kernel selection we use varies across architectures and we'll provide recommended instance families for your model/sequence lengths.
[06:20] Tom: any guidance on subnet sizing for autoscaling?
[06:24] Daniel: reserve IP capacity in subnets and use /20 or larger for clusters that scale; or use prefix delegation. we also recommend ENI warm pools for faster scaling.
[06:33] Lina: for the benchmark run, what's the minimal setup?
[06:36] Marcus: a dev VPC with 2 AZs, 2 instance types (one for runtime, one for worker), PrivateLink endpoint for control plane, S3 endpoint, KMS endpoint, and sample traffic script that reflects your QPS and batch size. We'll run both warm and cold cache passes.
[06:56] Priya: about KV cache coherence across nodes — if we scale to N nodes, is there a shared external cache or is it local only?
[07:04] Marcus: currently it's local-first with optional external Redis for shared cache; external caches add network round-trip and must be placed in low-latency subnets. we usually recommend node-local KV for latency sensitive workloads and Redis for larger multi-region consistency needs.
[07:22] Tom: can we do VPC peering instead of PrivateLink? pros/cons?
[07:27] Marcus: peering is simpler but means cross-account routing and exposure; PrivateLink is more controlled and isolates your VPC from our network. peering can be fine for low-sensitivity setups, but many enterprises prefer PrivateLink for compliance. peering also requires co-ordinating route tables and can complicate transitive routing.
[07:48] Alex: last question - how do you handle fallback if an AZ loses capacity?
[07:53] Marcus: we have routing policies and autoscaling across AZs; for strict latency SLOs we let you pin pools to AZs and provide failover to other pools (with expected latency increase). cushioned autoscaling and prioritized warm pools help reduce cold start impact.
[08:10] Sofia: ok let's recap next steps. Marcus, you'll share benchmark sheet and kernel notes. I'll upload diagrams and security docs. Lina will give us the VPC details and we'll schedule the in-VPC run.
[08:22] Priya: sounds good, thanks everyone.
[08:25] Sofia: thanks all, we'll follow up in CRM with links and invite for the benchmark slot.

End of transcript
